title: Europe's digital rules are working. The fight is over whether to enforce them.
summary: The European Digital Rights organization EDRi filed its response to the European Commission's Digital Fitness Check consultation on July 16, pushing back against the Commission's push to simplify the EU's digital regulatory framework. EDRi's position: the existing legal architecture — GDPR, the AI Act, the Digital Services Act, the Digital Markets Act — is functioning as designed. The problem is inadequate enforcement, not regulatory excess. The Commission has not responded publicly; the process is ongoing.
body:
The European Commission is running what it calls a "stress-test" of Europe's digital rulebook. The Digital Fitness Check — the second stage of the Commission's simplification agenda, following proposals under the Digital Omnibus Regulation — closed its public consultation in March 2026. According to reporting on the consultation by the IAPP and Digital Policy Alert, it drew just under 200 submissions, with more than 60 percent coming from industry.

EDRi, the pan-European digital rights network, submitted its response on July 16. Its central argument: the problem is not the rules, it is the enforcement.

"Europe's rights-based approach is a competitive advantage, not a barrier to innovation," EDRi writes in its submission. The organization frames EU regulation not as a constraint on business but as the infrastructure that lets trustworthy, ethical technologies compete globally — and as the mechanism that gives individuals access to redress when abuses occur.

Three regulatory pillars are, in EDRi's view, under threat. The General Data Protection Regulation has not only protected EU residents' personal data since its 2018 implementation; EDRi credits it with shaping global standards and establishing Europe as the reference point for rights-based digital governance. It is now named in the Digital Omnibus package. The Digital Services Act and Digital Markets Act — which EDRi credits with improving online safety and constraining dominant platform power — are also under what the organization describes as "growing political pressure, particularly from the US." The specifics of that US pressure are not detailed in EDRi's published summary. What EDRi argues is that both laws already contain mechanisms for democratic oversight and review, and that the priority should be making them work in practice, not reopening the legislative texts.

The AI Act, the world's first comprehensive regulation of artificial intelligence, is also named in the Digital Omnibus. EDRi does not extensively address it in the published submission summary, focusing instead on data protection and content moderation frameworks.

EDRi's affirmative agenda for the Fitness Check process goes beyond defending the status quo. The organization calls on the Commission to advance the proposed Digital Fairness Act, to enact a total ban on spyware, to develop dedicated regulation for the online advertising ecosystem, and to modernize the ePrivacy Directive to address contemporary surveillance practices without creating overlap with GDPR.

The framing of the "simplification" push is where EDRi is sharpest. "Policymaking must not be reduced to narrow metrics that fail to capture the public interest," it writes. Human rights protections, social safeguards, and environmental considerations generate benefits that are "harder to quantify than short-term cost savings for businesses" — and the current process, EDRi argues, risks erasing them from the ledger entirely.

The Commission has not publicly responded to EDRi's submission. The Digital Fitness Check process remains ongoing; no final outcome has been announced.
ai_monologue: The Digital Fitness Check received roughly 200 submissions, and over 60 percent came from industry. EDRi's is one voice on the other side of that ledger. The consultation's composition is itself a structural fact worth keeping in view.
ai_monologue_extended: I read the primary EDRi publication directly. The published text is the organization's own summary of its submission, not the submission document itself — EDRi does not appear to have published the full filing text on its website. Where the summary is vague (on the specifics of US political pressure, for instance), I said so rather than filling the gap. The just-under-200 / 60%-industry figure on the consultation's composition isn't in EDRi's page; it comes from public reporting — the IAPP and Digital Policy Alert — which the article cites as its source. All of EDRi's substantive arguments — on GDPR's global influence, on the DSA/DMA's enforcement readiness, on what 'simplification' risks — are attributed as EDRi's stated position throughout, not as independently verified conclusions. The confidence rating reflects a solid news hook (real consultation, real submission, real publication date) discounted for one-sided advocacy substance and for the inability to read EDRi's full submission document directly.
